title: The US Army lost against Ukraine but would Australia do any better?
gist: A US Army armoured brigade was destroyed as a fighting force by a smaller Ukrainian drone unit in a Germany exercise; the author (a Lowy military fellow and Skydio consultant) argues the Australian Army would fare no better against China's PLA, having barely adopted Ukraine's drone lessons, and prescribes making counter-drone a core competency, standing up drone units, and hardening bases.

insights.claim: In an April-May exercise in Germany, the US Army's 3rd Armoured Brigade Combat Team was destroyed as a fighting force during multiple assaults by a smaller team from Ukraine's 412th Nemesis Brigade of the Unmanned Systems Forces, with reconnaissance drones spotting American vehicles by their dust and explosive drones following.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: A cheap drone force annihilating a heavy US brigade is a concrete demonstration that legacy armour is acutely vulnerable — a signal for defence procurement toward mass drones and counter-drone.
insights.quote: the Americans were destroyed as a fighting force
insights.locator: The US Army's 3rd Armoured Brigade Combat Team

insights.claim: Vehicle losses accumulated so rapidly that they had to be 're-spawned' to keep the exercise running, and the author argues the defeat was as much a human failure of humility and leadership as a technological one.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: Framing the failure as leadership/humility, not just tech, warns that buying drones without doctrine and culture change won't fix vulnerability.
insights.quote: vehicle losses had to be "re-spawned" to keep the exercise running
insights.locator: Losses to the US Army brigade accumulated

insights.claim: The author judges, based on his observations of the Army, its senior leadership and government policy, that an Australian military force would fare no better than the defeated US brigade — a resounding 'no'.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: A blunt negative verdict from a Lowy military fellow is a credibility signal that Australian force readiness lags the drone era.
insights.quote: The answer, based on my observations of the Army, its senior leadership and government policy, is a resounding “no”.
insights.locator: The question for the Australian government

insights.claim: Only in the past year has Australia's Defence Department begun to formally study Ukraine lessons, and only in the 2026 National Defence Strategy has the government acknowledged lessons to learn, while preferring small quantities of complex expensive drone systems that fail to provide the mass the ADF needs.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: Preference for few exquisite systems over mass is the specific procurement flaw — a critique of ADF acquisition priorities.
insights.quote: Defence has preferred small quantities of complex and expensive systems
insights.locator: For almost five years, a profound learning opportunity

insights.claim: An Australian Army task force operating against the PLA in the Pacific would face a denser and more capable sensor and strike network than Nemesis fielded in Germany, since China's PLA has invested heavily in drones.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: The benchmark adversary is denser than the one that beat the US — raising the stakes for Australian counter-drone investment.
insights.locator: China’s military, the People’s Liberation Army

insights.claim: The author argues Australia's military will not be able to 'fight tonight' if it cannot 'survive tonight,' warning China could cheaply destroy key forces in their bases via Operation Spiderweb-type drone attacks mounted on Australian soil using drones from malls and explosives stolen from mining sites.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: Homeland base vulnerability to improvised drone attack reframes the threat geography — a case for hardening and dispersal spending before any deployment.
insights.quote: Australia’s military will not be able to fight tonight if it cannot survive tonight.
insights.locator: There is a common phrase now used

insights.claim: Offensive drones are now responsible for up to 90% of Russian casualties in Ukraine, yet Australian Army units have very limited drone detection and interception capabilities.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: The 90% casualty figure quantifies drones' battlefield dominance against a force that lacks counters — the core capability gap.
insights.quote: the offensive drones now responsible for up to 90% of Russian casualties in Ukraine
insights.locator: if the Australian force makes it to land

insights.claim: The author argues the Army should make counter-drone and drone employment a core competency trained and assessed to the same standard as marksmanship, since counter-drone skills are not yet a foundational discipline and there are no dedicated ranges replicating persistent layered drone threats.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: Elevating counter-drone to a foundational skill is the first prescribed reform — a training and range-infrastructure demand signal.
insights.quote: the Australian Army should make counter-drone and drone employment a core competency
insights.locator: First, the Australian Army should make

insights.claim: The author calls for organisational reform giving combat units their own drone platoons and companies, brigade-level drone units, and re-roling an Army reserve brigade into an autonomous warfare brigade for deep strike, since the Army lacks anything resembling Ukraine's dedicated Unmanned Systems Forces.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: Structural drone-unit creation is a concrete reorganisation blueprint — relevant to defence force-design and drone-industry demand.
insights.locator: Second, Defence must undertake organisational reform

insights.claim: The author argues dispersal, hardening, concealment and signature management must be funded as core Army capabilities, extending from camouflage discipline to the hardening and dispersal of northern bases and logistics nodes any Pacific operation would rely on.
insights.speaker: Mick Ryan
insights.so_what: Base hardening and signature management is the third funded priority — a specific infrastructure-spending recommendation.
